step1_summary.Chief complaint: Cough and sore throat for about a week

Symptoms.Onset: Sore throat started about a week ago (last Thursday or Friday), cough started 1-2 days later, shortness of breath started 3-4 days ago
Symptoms.Duration: About 7 days for sore throat, 6 days for cough, 3-4 days for shortness of breath
Symptoms.Severity: Sore throat and cough bad enough to keep patient off work for 3-4 days; shortness of breath mild to moderate, no rest dyspnea, but unusual and worrying
Symptoms.Type of cough: Dry cough, no sputum or blood
Symptoms.Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath, wheeze, mild chest pain, initial low-grade fever for first 3 days, intermittent headache
Symptoms.Aggravating/alleviating factors: Symptoms fairly constant throughout the day (cough not worse at night); symptoms variable, sometimes better, sometimes worse

step1_summary.Past medical history: None, no asthma, no history of clots
step1_summary.Medications/allergies: No current medications; allergic to peanuts

Family/social history.Smoking: Never smoker (smoked once or twice recreationally in past)
Family/social history.Family history: Mother had lung cancer; no other significant family illnesses
Family/social history.Travel history: No recent exotic travel; lived in US until 12 years ago, currently in UK

step1_summary.Vitals/exam findings: No physical exam findings mentioned except no lumps in neck, no rashes

V: Pulmonary embolism: Dry cough, shortness of breath, chest pain and recent onset symptoms could suggest PE, but no clear risk factors.
Pneumothorax: Chest pain and shortness of breath could fit, but no trauma or acute severe onset.
I: Viral upper respiratory infection: Classic features of sore throat, dry cough, fever, headache, and gradual symptom onset; shortness of breath and wheeze possible with viral bronchitis or reactive airway.
Acute bronchitis: Dry cough, wheeze, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, typical course about 1-2 weeks.
Pneumonia (atypical): Instead of productive cough, dry cough less common but possible; fever initially present.
N: Lung cancer: Family history is positive, shortness of breath and cough could be symptoms, but acute onset and young age less typical.
D: Post-viral reactive airway disease: Following viral illness, some patients develop wheeze and breathing difficulty.
Vitamin D deficiency related respiratory symptoms: Unlikely acute, but included.
I2: Allergic reaction: Peanut allergy history, though no current allergic symptoms evident.
Drug-induced cough: No medications currently used.
C: Asthma: Patient denies history but new adult onset asthma possible with dry cough, wheeze, shortness of breath.
Congenital airway abnormality: No prior symptoms or history.
A: Allergic airway inflammation: Wheeze and cough possible from allergy, but no mention of triggers or rhinitis.
Autoimmune disease such as sarcoidosis: Unlikely with acute presentation and lack of other systemic symptoms.
T: Chest trauma: No trauma history; unlikely.
Foreign body aspiration: No history of choking.
E: Thyroid disease causing cough and dyspnea: No other features.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (likely viral bronchitis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Typical progression of sore throat, dry cough, mild fever initially that resolved; wheeze and mild chest pain could be from inflammation; no alarming features such as hemoptysis, high fever, or weight loss; patient improving but with occasional worsening.
supporting_evidence: Gradual symptom progression starting with sore throat
Dry cough with no sputum or blood
Shortness of breath mild and only on exertion
No systemic signs like weight loss
opposing_evidence: Persistent symptoms for a week with waxing and waning
Wheezing and chest pain less common but possible

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: New onset asthma or reactive airway disease post-viral infection
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath without prior asthma history could be reactive airway disease following viral infection; no history of asthma but adult onset is possible.
supporting_evidence: New wheeze and shortness of breath
No prior asthma but recent viral illness
opposing_evidence: Relatively mild symptoms not causing exercise limitation
